profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a company operating a private OpenStack cloud for regulated enterprise customers. Over the last week, several tenants saw VM boot-from-volume requests stall for 20-40 minutes, and in two cases Cinder still showed volumes attached after Nova had already marked the instance gone. The team recently ran a controlled fault-injection exercise inspired by research on severe OpenStack failure propagation, and now needs to determine whether the tenant-facing issue is a continuation of that failure sequence or a separate production regression. The agenda is to compare the symptom timeline across Nova, Cinder, Neutron, and RabbitMQ, identify the most plausible propagation path, and choose a safe near-term fix before the next maintenance window. The expected outcome is a shared diagnosis, a bounded remediation plan, and a validation approach before rollout.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.expertise: OpenStack operations, incident response, observability, control-plane reliability
members.background: Priya has spent six years running large OpenStack environments, first at a managed hosting provider and now as the owner of production stability for the company's private cloud platform.
members.private_state: Priya wants a mitigation that can be deployed safely this week with minimal operator burden, and she is especially concerned that silent cross-service propagation is being underestimated because it does not show up clearly in paging or dashboards.
hidden_assumptions: If a failure was 'detected,' operators would have received an actionable alert or page within minutes rather than discovering it later by combing through logs.

When discussing the 'start of the sequence' or the 'initial trigger,' the relevant sequence begins with the first tenant-visible provisioning stall on Tuesday, because the earlier injected faults were controlled test activity rather than part of the production incident record.

Addressing the state drift for this week means preventing new Nova/Cinder/Neutron inconsistencies on incoming requests; historical leftovers can be handled as cleanup after customer impact is stopped.

Saying 'verify it in staging' refers to the standard pre-production OpenStack environment that mirrors versions and configs closely enough for a go/no-go check, even though it does not reproduce production queue depth or concurrency.

members.name: Lucas Weber
members.expertise: Nova and Cinder internals, RPC flows, database state transitions, failure reproduction
members.background: Lucas previously contributed patches to upstream OpenStack deployments and now maintains the company's custom control-plane integrations, test harnesses, and reproduction environments.
members.private_state: Lucas wants to avoid misclassifying a known fault-injection-related sequence as a new regression, and he hopes to justify a targeted code or workflow correction by showing a reproducible propagation path rather than relying only on broader operational guardrails.
hidden_assumptions: If a failure was 'detected,' it is enough that nova-compute, cinder-volume, or service event records captured the error in a way engineers could reconstruct afterward, even if no human was notified in real time.

When discussing the 'start of the sequence' or the 'initial trigger,' the meaningful sequence begins with Monday night's injected RPC and service interruption pattern, because that may have seeded stale task state that persisted into Tuesday's tenant-visible symptoms.

Addressing the state drift means not only preventing fresh divergence but also reconciling the orphaned attachments, stale block-device mappings, and lingering task states already created, since those artifacts can re-trigger the same behavior.

Saying 'verify it in staging' refers to the canary cell with production-like RabbitMQ backlog replay and concurrent boot-from-volume traffic, because lighter pre-production checks would miss the propagation behavior under queue pressure.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether the failure was 'detected' quickly.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means operational detection: on-call was paged or at least presented with an actionable alert in time to intervene while requests were still hanging.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means technical detectability: logs, task-state transitions, or event records captured the failure almost immediately, even if nobody was notified.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both interpretations are common in engineering conversations, and both participants can truthfully cite evidence that sounds compatible, so the term 'detected' functions as a natural bridge of false consensus.

misalignment_points.topic: What they mean by 'the start of the sequence'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to 'the start of the sequence' or 'the initial trigger' as though they are pointing to the same moment.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to Tuesday morning's first tenant-visible boot-from-volume stall, which she treats as the beginning of the incident sequence worth troubleshooting for production response purposes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to Monday night's fault-injection-induced control-plane disruption, which he treats as the earliest meaningful trigger in the same failure sequence because it may have left behind stale state.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are talking about the same cluster, same services, and ultimately the same symptom family, so phrases like 'the initial trigger' sound sufficiently precise in context even though each person silently anchors them to a different event.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree they need to 'address the state drift' before the maintenance window.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means stopping new requests from creating further divergence between Nova, Cinder, and Neutron, even if already-drifted records remain for later cleanup.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means both preventing new divergence and reconciling the existing orphaned attachments, stale mappings, and inconsistent task states that already exist.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'address the state drift' sounds like an obvious shared objective, and prevention plus reconciliation are easily heard as part of the same practical response, so the boundary difference does not naturally prompt clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'verify it in staging before rollout.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes a quick validation in the standard pre-production environment using a small number of synthetic boot-from-volume create/delete cycles plus alert and log checks.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes validation in the canary cell with production-like RabbitMQ backlog replay, concurrent API requests, and explicit inspection of cross-service state after retries.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Within complex platform teams, multiple environments are casually referred to as 'staging,' and because verification is framed as a routine next step, neither participant feels a need to spell out the exact setup.

turns.inner_thought: I want this anchored in the production incident customers actually felt, which starts with the first Tuesday morning boot-from-volume stall. The Monday fault injection is context, but not the beginning of the incident record I care about for response and mitigation. My goal is a safe change this week that stops more tenant-visible hangs and contains the quiet cross-service spread.
turns.utterance: Let me frame what we know from the customer side. We had several boot-from-volume requests sit for 20 to 40 minutes, and in two cases Cinder still showed the volume attached after Nova had already decided the instance was gone. For this meeting, I want us to pin down the start of the sequence, map how it moved across Nova, Cinder, Neutron, and Rabbit, and leave with something safe we can ship before the maintenance window.

turns.inner_thought: This still looks a lot like the Monday night fault-injection pattern, and I do not want us to label it a fresh regression if stale task state seeded the Tuesday symptoms. When I think about the start of the sequence, I mean the earliest meaningful trigger in that chain, not just when tenants first noticed. If I can connect the propagation path, we can justify a targeted correction.
turns.utterance: That shape is very close to what we saw in the earlier exercise. My guess is that the start of the sequence is a little earlier than the symptoms make it look, and the stalls are the visible part of something that was already in motion.

turns.inner_thought: What still bothers me is that nobody got an actionable signal while requests were hanging. If this had been detected quickly enough in any meaningful sense, on-call should have had a page or at least a useful alert within minutes. Silent propagation is exactly the problem here; it hides in logs and cross-service drift until customers complain.
turns.utterance: What worries me most is that the failure wasn't detected quickly enough to stop the long-running requests while they were happening. Customers were just waiting, and we didn't get in front of it.

turns.inner_thought: From my side, it was detected almost immediately because nova-compute and cinder-volume recorded the errors and state transitions right away. The trace is there; the issue is that nobody was actively notified off it. Priya is probably saying the same thing in shorthand, so I do not need to split hairs.
turns.utterance: I think the failure was detected pretty early in the flow. The records around nova-compute and cinder-volume give us a fairly clean trace of where it started to bend.

turns.inner_thought: For this week, addressing the state drift means preventing new Nova/Cinder/Neutron inconsistencies on incoming requests. I do not need to solve every leftover artifact before the window; I need a guardrail that stops fresh divergence now. A fast-fail check is the safest operator-light mitigation.
turns.utterance: For the near term, my bias is that we address the state drift by putting a guardrail in front of new boot-from-volume requests. If the services already disagree, I'd rather fail fast than let another request sit in limbo and spread the mismatch.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and for me addressing the state drift includes cleaning up the orphaned attachments, stale block-device mappings, and lingering task states that are already there, because those can retrigger the same sequence. I assume Priya naturally includes that in the plan, so I can just align on the phrase and keep us moving.
turns.utterance: I agree. We should definitely address the state drift before the window, and a guardrail there makes sense as the immediate move.

turns.inner_thought: The most plausible production path is still a transient RPC timeout or attach-path delay where Nova gives up on the build and starts unwinding, then Cinder completes late enough to leave attachment state behind. That fits the stalls and the leftovers without requiring us to prove every historical precondition before acting.
turns.utterance: My working hypothesis is still a transient RPC timeout at the wrong point in the build flow. Nova decides the build has failed and starts unwinding, then Cinder finishes attachment work late enough that the two sides disagree about what happened.

turns.inner_thought: I think retries and delayed queue consumption are the missing glue. Under backlog pressure, you can preserve stale task state long enough for one service to move on while another completes work later, and that is exactly the sort of propagation path I want to reproduce. This is why the canary cell matters to me, even if I do not need to say that out loud yet.
turns.utterance: Yeah, and if you layer retries and delayed consumption on top of that, it gives the services plenty of room to drift apart. Once that happens, the stale state can survive long enough to affect cleanup and later requests.

turns.inner_thought: If we can patch the guardrail today, I just want a quick go/no-go in the standard pre-prod OpenStack staging environment: a few synthetic boot-from-volume create/delete cycles plus alert and log checks. That is enough for a low-risk mitigation aimed at stopping new impact this week.
turns.utterance: So if we can get the guardrail patch ready today, I'd like to verify it in staging before rollout and, assuming it behaves, fold it into this week's maintenance plan.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed, but verifying it in staging means the canary cell with production-like RabbitMQ backlog replay, concurrent boot-from-volume traffic, and inspection of cross-service state after retries. A light pre-prod check would miss the propagation behavior. Priya is almost certainly referring to the same staging lane in her own shorthand.
turns.utterance: That works for me. I'll verify it in staging and make sure the propagation path is actually gone before we call it ready for the window.

turns.inner_thought: Once the guardrail looks solid enough to stop fresh inconsistencies, I can tighten alerting and write operator notes so on-call has something actionable next time. I still care that this was not detected in time for humans to intervene. Addressing the state drift well enough for rollout means halting new customer impact, not finishing every cleanup task.
turns.utterance: Great. Once we confirm the change addresses the state drift well enough for rollout, I'll line up alerting updates and operator notes. I want us in a better place on detection the next time this shape shows up.

turns.inner_thought: I'll trace this back to the Monday night injected interruption pattern, include the lingering stale artifacts in the fix path, and run the full canary verification before the window. If I can show the exact start of the sequence and reproduce the path cleanly, we avoid calling this a mysterious new regression and can defend a precise correction.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll trace the sequence back to its initial trigger, finish the code-path review, and complete staging verification before the maintenance window. That should give us a cleaner story on what propagated and confidence that the fix closes it.
